questions.prompt: An incremental feed receiver has applied messages 1..N correctly, then silently misapplies message N+1 and keeps processing. What is the consequence?
options: Its book is wrong from N+1 onward and stays wrong indefinitely, because the state is a function of every message ever processed.
The error is confined to N+1 and washes out once that price level is next deleted and re-added by a later feed message.
The next few incremental messages restate the affected level from their own contents, so the book self-corrects within a second.
The sequence-number check catches the divergence, because sequence validation covers the applied state and not merely arrival order.
questions.explanation: Incremental encoding buys its bandwidth advantage by making the receiver stateful and history-dependent, so a single misapplied message corrupts the replica permanently and silently. The tempting answer is the one crediting the sequence check with catching it: sequence numbers prove that messages arrived in order, not that they were applied correctly, so a semantic misapplication passes every sequence test. Nor does a delta feed restate levels — that is precisely what a snapshot does and an incremental does not.

questions.prompt: A price-level aggregated feed loses one `New, level=2` message. The handler keeps applying subsequent level-indexed updates. What state results?
options: A structurally valid book — prices ordered, sizes positive — in which every level below the loss is wrong, with no intrinsic error signal.
A book that fails its own ordering invariant immediately, because a missing insert leaves two entries competing for one level index.
A book correct everywhere except level 2, because level indices are absolute positions that the feed restates on each message.
A book with an empty slot at level 2 that stays visibly short until the next Delete action rebalances the level count.
questions.explanation: Level indices are positional and relative: a missed insert means every later index is applied one level off, and the result is a perfectly well-formed book that is simply not the exchange's book. The most tempting distractor is the 'correct except at level 2' answer, whose premise — that the message carries a price — is true, but the index is still relative, so the damage propagates downward rather than staying local. This absence of any self-check is exactly why price-level feeds carry a per-instrument `RptSeq` that must be validated.

questions.prompt: A candidate asserts that order-by-order and price-level feeds are equally exposed to silent corruption from one lost message. Where does the claim break down?
options: Order-by-order updates cite an exchange order reference, so an update for an unknown reference is direct proof of a gap; level indices offer no such check.
Price-level feeds carry a per-instrument `RptSeq`, so one lost message cannot corrupt their book even when the sequence check is omitted entirely.
Both styles restate absolute levels on every message, so a lost update is simply overwritten by the next message touching the same instrument.
Order-by-order feeds are the more fragile of the two, because a lost Add leaves later Execute messages with no way to signal the missing order.
questions.explanation: The self-checking property is real and asymmetric: an order-by-order handler that receives a Delete or Execute for a reference it has never seen has proof of prior loss, whereas a price-level handler applying a shifted index has nothing to complain about. The `RptSeq` answer has a true premise — those feeds do carry one — but the conclusion inverts the point: `RptSeq` is mandatory precisely because the message content provides no protection on its own. The 'order-by-order is more fragile' option states the detection mechanism backwards; an unresolvable reference is the signal, not a blind spot.

questions.prompt: A normalizer treats CME-style Change quantities as deltas when the venue in fact sends new absolute quantities. What is the diagnostic signature?
options: Sizes drift in a direction that correlates with activity and the book diverges from the exchange's periodic checksum within seconds of the open.
Sizes stay exact until the first Delete arrives, which then removes more quantity than the level ever held and drives that level negative.
Divergence appears only on instruments that use Replace messages, because Replace is the sole action whose payload carries a quantity field.
Nothing is observable until the close, when the exchange's end-of-session snapshot is the first message to restate absolute level sizes.
questions.explanation: Absolute-versus-delta is the classic normalization bug: the error accumulates on every update, so quantities either march toward zero or grow without bound at a rate proportional to instrument activity, and the exchange checksum catches it almost immediately. The 'exact until the first Delete' answer is tempting because a size error does eventually surface as an impossible removal, but the divergence begins with the very first Change, long before any Delete. Replace is not the only action carrying quantity, and waiting for a closing snapshot would mean trading a wrong book all day.

questions.prompt: Why is a snapshot that carries no sequence anchor unusable for recovery?
options: You cannot know which incrementals it already reflects, so the only use is to discard the buffer and hope, silently losing the whole window.
The channel numbering is independent of the incremental feed, so an unanchored snapshot cannot be matched to the right instrument at all.
The receiver cannot verify the snapshot's checksum, so a corrupted body would install silently and never be detected by any later check.
The level list cannot be sorted without an anchor, because the ordering of levels in a snapshot body is derived from the sequence number.
questions.explanation: The anchor (`LastMsgSeqNumProcessed`, or a per-instrument `RptSeq`) is what lets the receiver split its buffer into 'already included' and 'still to apply'; without it there is no defensible way to compose snapshot and deltas. The checksum answer is the closest miss — integrity and sequence anchoring are different properties, and a body that is byte-perfect is still unusable if you cannot place it in time. Instrument identity and level ordering come from the snapshot's own fields, not from the sequence number.

questions.prompt: A network event leaves a thousand subscribers needing recovery at the same instant. How do the two snapshot delivery models behave?
options: The cyclic multicast channel is unaffected because its cost is independent of subscriber count, while the request/reply service saturates exactly when it is most needed.
Both degrade in proportion to subscriber count, because the exchange must assemble a distinct snapshot message per recovering client under either model.
The request/reply service copes better under load, because unicast TCP retransmits its own losses whereas the multicast cycle drops packets under congestion.
The cyclic channel saturates first, because each recovering client must join the group and the exchange emits one additional cycle for every joiner.
questions.explanation: A cyclic snapshot channel is a passive multicast subscription: one publisher, one stream, so a thousand recoverers cost the exchange no more than one, and recovery time is bounded by the cycle. The 'unicast TCP is more reliable' answer has a true premise — TCP does retransmit — but the conclusion ignores that the request/reply service is a rate-limited shared resource that is overwhelmed by exactly the mass-recovery event in question. Multicast fan-out is done in the network, so extra joiners do not multiply the publisher's work.

questions.prompt: Your book maintains full depth, but the snapshot channel publishes only the top ten levels. How should recovery handle the levels below ten?
options: Install the ten levels and mark everything deeper as unknown, because an unknown level and an empty level are genuinely different states.
Install the ten levels and treat everything deeper as empty, which is conservative because it can only ever understate the liquidity present.
Discard the snapshot and wait for a full-depth cycle, because a depth-truncated snapshot cannot carry a valid sequence anchor for the book.
Install the ten levels and retain the pre-gap contents below level ten, which remain valid because the snapshot does not restate them.
questions.explanation: A truncated snapshot leaves you with a partial book, and the honest representation is that depth beyond the published limit is unknown, so downstream logic can refuse to use it rather than reason on a fiction. The 'treat deeper as empty, it is conservative' option is the tempting one: understating liquidity is not a safe error — a strategy that believes the book is thin will size and price differently, and the mistake is invisible. Keeping stale pre-gap depth is worse still, since that content is precisely what the gap made untrustworthy, and truncation has nothing to do with whether the anchor is valid.

questions.prompt: Recovery has been buffering since F = 5,001. A snapshot arrives with `LastMsgSeqNumProcessed` = 4,998. What is the correct action?
options: Discard the snapshot and keep buffering, because 4,998 is below F − 1 and messages 4,999 and 5,000 sit in neither the snapshot nor the buffer.
Install it and apply the entire buffer, since a snapshot predating F cannot possibly double-count any message the buffer is already holding.
Install it and apply buffered messages above 4,998, since the buffer's own contiguity guarantees that no hole can exist below its first entry.
Discard the buffer, install the snapshot, and resume from the next live message, since a freshly published snapshot supersedes any buffered state.
questions.explanation: The rule is X >= F − 1; here X = 4,998 and F − 1 = 5,000, so two messages exist that the snapshot does not cover and the buffer never captured — installing it would create a permanent silent hole. The 'cannot double-count' answer is the most seductive because its premise is true: an early snapshot really does avoid overlap. But the failure mode being guarded against is the opposite one, a hole rather than an overlap. Discarding the buffer instead would throw away valid post-snapshot updates and still leave the hole.

questions.prompt: The first buffered message is F = 8,400 and a snapshot arrives with `LastMsgSeqNumProcessed` = 8,399. What should the receiver do?
options: Install it, discard nothing from the buffer, apply the buffer from 8,400 onward, and mark the instrument LIVE — the snapshot abuts the buffer exactly.
Discard it and wait for the next cycle, because a usable snapshot must cover at least the first buffered message, that is X >= F rather than F − 1.
Install it but request retransmission of 8,400 first, because a snapshot ending one short of F cannot prove that the buffer starts contiguously.
Install it and drop buffered messages up to and including 8,400, because the anchor is exclusive and already accounts for the first buffered entry.
questions.explanation: X = F − 1 is the ideal case: the snapshot covers everything strictly before the buffer and the buffer covers everything from F on, with neither hole nor overlap. The X >= F variant is the classic off-by-one and the most tempting wrong answer — it rejects perfectly good snapshots and costs a whole extra recovery cycle every time. Requesting retransmission of 8,400 asks for a message already in hand, and treating the anchor as exclusive would discard 8,400 and open a one-message hole.

questions.prompt: Why must the handler begin buffering incrementals before it starts waiting for or requesting a snapshot?
options: Otherwise messages arriving between the snapshot's cut-off and the start of buffering are lost permanently, and nothing in the algorithm detects the loss.
Otherwise the first buffered sequence F is unknown, so the receiver cannot size the arbitration window it applies to the incremental channel.
Otherwise the snapshot arrives before any buffer exists and must be dropped, which costs one extra recovery cycle but nothing worse than that.
Otherwise the exchange rejects the request, because a snapshot request must state the sequence number the client has already begun buffering.
questions.explanation: Reversing the order creates a race with no detector: the window between the snapshot's cut-off and the start of buffering is simply missing, and because both the snapshot and the later buffer look internally consistent, the resulting book is confidently wrong. The 'costs one extra cycle' answer is the tempting understatement — it treats a silent correctness hole as a mere latency penalty. The arbitration window is derived from measured inter-feed skew and has nothing to do with F.

questions.prompt: A liquid instrument is recovering, and the bounded recovery buffer fills before any usable snapshot arrives. What is the correct behaviour?
options: Abandon this attempt, restart recovery with a fresh F, and increment an explicit counter so the event is visible in operations.
Evict the oldest buffered messages to make room, since the eventual snapshot will almost certainly cover the sequences being dropped.
Apply the buffered messages to the pre-gap book to free space, then continue buffering from the current live sequence number.
Grow the buffer on demand without limit, because correctness requires that no message arriving after the gap is ever discarded.
questions.explanation: Overflow means this recovery attempt cannot complete correctly, so the honest response is to restart it from a new F and count the occurrence — correct, explicit, and observable. The 'grow without limit' answer is the strongest distractor because its premise is a real rule of gap recovery, but an unbounded buffer under a 5 s cycle at 50 k msg/s is an unbounded memory commitment, and the rule against discarding applies within an attempt, not across a failed one. Evicting the oldest entries silently reintroduces the very hole the buffer exists to prevent, and applying deltas to a book known to be wrong compounds the corruption.

questions.prompt: `expected_` is 9,124 when a packet arrives beginning at sequence 9,120 and carrying eight messages. What is the correct handling?
options: Process only messages 9,124 through 9,127, deriving each message's sequence as packet_seq plus index, then advance `expected_` to 9,128.
Drop the packet entirely, because its starting sequence is below `expected_` and the duplicate rule removes anything that begins in the past.
Process the packet in full, because re-applying four already-seen messages is idempotent once the book has recorded their order references.
Hold the packet in the reorder buffer until a packet beginning exactly at 9,124 arrives, then apply the two of them in sequence order.
questions.explanation: This is the partial-overlap case: the packet straddles `expected_`, so the only correct granularity is per message, which requires deriving each message's own sequence from the packet sequence plus its index. Dropping it wholesale is the most common error and re-creates the very gap the packet would have filled. Processing it whole double-applies four messages, and book updates are emphatically not idempotent — a repeated Execute reduces size twice.

questions.prompt: At the open, message rates run far above the daily average, a large gap appears, and `rx_missed_errors` is climbing on your NIC. What is the right response?
options: Resync from the snapshot channel and accept losing the first seconds, because retransmission adds load exactly where you have no headroom left.
Request retransmission at once, because a gap measured in wall-clock terms is short at the open and retransmission always beats a snapshot cycle.
Keep waiting on the arbitration window until the B feed fills the gap, because a receive-ring overflow can only ever affect one of the two ports.
Disable the instrument for the remainder of the session, because a gap during the open means the book cannot be trusted for the rest of the day.
questions.explanation: Climbing `rx_missed_errors` correlated with a rate spike identifies the loss as your own receive ring overflowing, not the network, and a retransmission request would add inbound traffic to a host that is already dropping packets. The 'retransmission is always faster' answer is the tempting one: it is true for small gaps on a healthy host, but the premise fails here because the bottleneck is your own ingress, and a snapshot resync is a passive subscription that costs no extra request traffic. Waiting on B is no help when the overflow is host-side and both rings are under the same burst.

questions.prompt: Gaps appear on the A feed and the B feed at exactly the same sequence numbers. What does this establish?
options: The loss is upstream of the path split — the exchange publisher or a shared segment — so nothing on your side of the split will repair it.
Your receive ring is overflowing, because a host-side drop is the only mechanism that can affect two physically disjoint paths at once.
The arbitration window is set too short, so B's copies are being declared missing well before they actually arrive at the merge point.
The two feeds have drifted into separate sequence spaces, so `expected_` must be tracked per feed rather than shared across the merge.
questions.explanation: A and B traverse disjoint paths, so identical sequence loss on both cannot be a path event by construction — it must predate the split, which leaves the publisher or a shared upstream segment, and retransmission or snapshot is the only recovery. The receive-ring answer is the plausible near-miss: ring overflow is a real cause of correlated loss across ports on one host, but it does not produce byte-identical sequence ranges the way a publisher drop does, and it would show up in `rx_missed_errors`. A/B feeds share one sequence space by design, which is what makes arbitration possible at all.

questions.prompt: On detecting a 12-message gap, a handler discards every subsequent incremental until recovery completes. What is wrong with that?
options: Those messages are valid and are needed at the install step of snapshot-plus-delta, so discarding them turns a 12-message gap into a full resync.
Nothing is wrong for correctness; the instrument merely stays non-LIVE slightly longer than a design that buffered them would have required.
Nothing is wrong at all, because the snapshot restates the entire book and therefore supersedes every message that arrived after the gap.
The discards corrupt the duplicate counter, because `expected_` cannot advance past the gap while post-gap messages are being thrown away.
questions.explanation: Post-gap messages are perfectly good data; the recovery algorithm consumes them at step 4, applying everything above the snapshot's anchor. The 'only a latency cost' answer is the tempting one, and it is wrong on its own terms: without the buffer the snapshot can never abut anything, so every attempt fails the X >= F − 1 test and recovery degrades from a small buffered fill into repeated full cycles. A snapshot does restate the book, but only as of its anchor — everything after it still has to come from the buffer.

questions.prompt: Why must the duplicate-suppression check run before decoding rather than after it?
options: With A/B feeds roughly half of all packets are duplicates, so decoding first doubles decode work for messages that are immediately discarded.
Decoding rewrites the sequence field in place during normalization, so a decoded duplicate can no longer be compared against `expected_` at all.
The suppression check hashes the raw payload bytes, and decoding consumes that buffer without preserving the bytes the hash requires.
Decoders hold per-message scratch state that is not reentrant, so passing a duplicate through one corrupts the in-flight primary message.
questions.explanation: On a two-feed setup the second copy of every message is a duplicate, so dedup-before-decode removes about half the decode work — roughly a third more feed-handler throughput for a single integer comparison. The hashing answer is the closest miss: content hashing does need the raw bytes, but sequence-based suppression is the correct default and needs only the packet header, so the argument for ordering rests on cost rather than on hash inputs. Decoding neither mutates the wire sequence nor requires reentrancy here.

questions.prompt: A venue's feed carries no sequence numbers at all. What is the honest assessment of content-hash duplicate suppression as the remedy?
options: It is a probabilistic fallback whose collisions silently drop real messages and which cannot separate a duplicate from a genuinely repeated print.
It is equivalent to sequence-based suppression provided the hash is 64 bits wide and the recent-hash window exceeds the maximum inter-feed skew.
It is superior for arbitration, because identical payloads on the two feeds are matched to each other even when the paths reorder packets badly.
It is unnecessary work, because two byte-identical trade prints cannot occur in one session, so any repeated payload is a duplicate by definition.
questions.explanation: Content hashing costs a hash and a lookup per message, bounds its window arbitrarily, and is exact in neither direction: a collision drops a real message, and two legitimately identical trade prints are indistinguishable from one duplicated print. The 'unnecessary, identical prints cannot occur' option states the failure backwards — repeated identical prints are exactly the case that breaks the scheme. Widening the hash reduces collision probability without making the technique exact, so the equivalence claim fails; the correct conclusion is that a protocol lacking sequence numbers is itself the defect.

questions.prompt: A feed handler subscribed to several multicast channels keeps one global `expected_` counter for duplicate suppression. Why is this wrong?
options: Sequence spaces are per channel, so one channel's numbering carries no meaning against another's and the comparison drops or accepts arbitrarily.
It is correct but slow, because the shared counter is contended whenever more than one channel is being polled from the same receive loop.
It works only when every channel is served by one exchange gateway, which is the usual arrangement for the two halves of an A/B feed pair.
It is adequate for duplicates but breaks gap detection, because gaps are tracked per instrument whereas duplicates are counted per packet.
questions.explanation: Each channel numbers its own stream from its own origin, so comparing a packet from channel 7 against a counter last advanced by channel 3 is a comparison between unrelated integers: some genuine messages are silently dropped as 'old' and some real duplicates pass through. The contention answer is tempting but false on its premise — the arbitrator is single-writer with both feeds polled by one thread, so there is no contention to speak of, and the defect is correctness rather than speed. A and B of one pair do share a sequence space, which is a different fact from channels sharing one.

questions.prompt: Your retransmission-request rate is high and nearly every response is discarded as a duplicate on arrival. What is the diagnosis?
options: The arbitration window is too short, so ordinary inter-feed skew is being read as a gap before the second feed's copy has arrived.
The arbitration window is too long, so real gaps sit undetected until the timer expires and requests are issued after B already resolved them.
The retransmission service is replaying a stale window, so by design its responses fall below `expected_` and are rejected as old copies.
A switch on the B path is duplicating packets, so each retransmission response collides with an extra live copy of the same messages.
questions.explanation: That symptom pair — many requests, nearly all responses discarded — is the signature of declaring a gap before the arbitration window has elapsed: the slower feed delivers the missing packet, `expected_` advances, and the response you asked for arrives already stale. The 'window is too long' option is the most tempting because its premise is a genuine failure mode, but it produces the opposite signature, namely late detection and undetected staleness rather than a storm of redundant requests. Path-level duplication would inflate the duplicate count without driving the request rate at all.

questions.prompt: Why take whichever A/B copy arrives first, per packet, rather than designating A as primary with failover to B?
options: First arrival yields min-of-two path latency on every packet and removes a failover decision that can flap; a designated primary forfeits both.
First arrival is mandatory because the two groups run independent sequence spaces that only an explicit merge step is able to reconcile.
A designated primary doubles the reorder buffer, because every B packet must be retained until A's copy is confirmed to be missing entirely.
A designated primary is unsafe because exchanges make no guarantee that the B group carries the same message stream that A carries.
questions.explanation: Because path latencies differ by hundreds of nanoseconds to a few microseconds and the winner varies packet by packet, taking first arrival is a free latency improvement on top of the reliability gain, and it needs no failover state machine to flap. The 'B may not carry the same stream' answer inverts the premise of arbitration — the two groups carry identical message streams over disjoint paths, which is exactly why the merge works. They also share one sequence space, so the independent-numbering claim is false as well.

questions.prompt: Against which failure does A/B arbitration provide essentially no protection?
options: A message the exchange's own publisher never emitted on either group, leaving both feeds identically short at the same sequence.
A congested switch port on the A path that discards a burst of packets during the first minute of the trading session.
A NIC receive-ring overflow on the single port that serves one of the two feeds while the other port keeps draining normally.
A marginal optic on one of the two paths that corrupts and drops packets at a low but persistent rate through the day.
questions.explanation: Arbitration works because losses are path-specific and therefore independent, so anything that happens upstream of the split — a publisher drop, a shared segment — is present in neither copy and must be recovered by retransmission or snapshot. Congested ports, single-port ring overflows, and a bad optic are all path-local and are precisely the cases arbitration eliminates at zero recovery latency, which is why offering any of them here is the natural mistake. Identical gaps on both feeds at identical sequences are the diagnostic fingerprint of the upstream case.

questions.prompt: Feed A's win rate falls from about 50% to 4% over a week while both feeds still report zero lost packets. What does this mean?
options: The A path is degrading; win rate leads packet loss by a wide margin, so investigate that path before it starts dropping anything.
The merge has become effectively single-feed, so B should be promoted to primary and A removed from the arbitration set until repaired.
Nothing is wrong: win rate merely reflects which ring the poll loop happens to service first and carries no information about path health.
The A path's timestamps have drifted late relative to B's, so the PTP client needs recalibration and the win rate then returns to parity.
questions.explanation: Win rate — how often each feed delivers a message first — is a continuous measure of relative path latency, so a collapse from parity to a few percent means A has acquired persistent extra delay, and that shows up long before the path starts losing packets. The 'promote B to primary' answer is tempting because it reacts to real evidence, but the correct arbitration design never designates a primary; the merge already ignores the slow feed automatically, and the useful action is to fix the path. Win rate is derived from actual arrival order, not from which ring is polled first, and it is unaffected by timestamp calibration.

questions.prompt: Two merged streams deliver events carrying equal sequence numbers and equal exchange timestamps. How must a deterministic merge order them?
options: By a further documented key such as channel id and then instrument id, so the resulting order is fixed independently of arrival.
By arrival time at the receiver, which is the only tie-break still available once both of the explicit ordering keys compare equal.
By the order in which the poll loop observed them, recorded into the output stream so that a later replay can reproduce the choice.
By whichever stream has processed fewer messages so far, a rule that balances the two inputs and is stable from one run to the next.
questions.explanation: Every tie must have a defined winner drawn from the data itself; the standard comparator falls through sequence, then exchange timestamp, then channel, then instrument, which makes the merge a pure function of its inputs. The 'record the arrival order into the output' option is the subtle one — recording a timing decision as an input is a legitimate technique for unavoidable real-time behaviour, but here an explicit data key exists, so admitting arrival order at all makes the primary and its hot standby diverge. A rule keyed on messages-processed-so-far depends on upstream arrival history and is therefore not stable either.

questions.prompt: Book updates are published by iterating an `unordered_map` of price levels. What is the real problem with that?
options: Output order depends on insertion history, hash seed, and capacity, so two instances of one build diverge while every unit test still passes.
Iteration over an open-addressed table is slower than over an ordered container at book depth, making the publish stage the latency bottleneck.
The container can rehash part-way through an iteration and emit one level twice, which downstream consumers then count as a duplicate update.
Iteration order is fixed for a given binary, so behaviour is deterministic locally and changes only when the compiler or library is upgraded.
questions.explanation: This is a genuine non-determinism that unit tests never catch, because a single process comparing against itself is self-consistent; it surfaces only when a primary and a hot standby are compared and their books disagree despite identical inputs. The 'deterministic for a given binary' option is the most tempting: the hash function is fixed per build, but bucket order also depends on the insertion sequence and on rehash history, both of which differ between two instances that took different paths through the day. The fix is an ordered structure or an explicit sorted index for anything observable.

questions.prompt: In differential replay, why hash the book state after every applied message rather than once at the end of the capture?
options: The first sequence number at which two runs disagree localizes the defect to a single message, turning a pass/fail signal into a debugging tool.
End-of-run hashes can coincide by chance when two errors compensate, so per-message hashing is the only way to detect divergence at all.
Per-message hashing keeps the hashed input small enough to remain resident in L1, which a whole-capture hash could never manage to do.
A final hash cannot be computed until the book is quiesced, and a book fed from a full trading day's capture never reaches that state.
questions.explanation: Both schemes detect that a divergence happened; only the per-message hash tells you where, and the difference between 'the build changed something' and 'message 4,118,203 changed something' is the difference between a red test and a fixed bug. The compensating-errors answer is the most tempting because such cancellation is conceivable, but a per-message hash is not the only way to detect divergence — a final hash catches the overwhelming majority — so the claim overstates its case. Hash locality and quiescence are not real constraints on a canonical state hash.

questions.prompt: Why can a handler not treat 'no messages for this instrument recently' as evidence that the feed has gone stale?
options: A genuinely quiet instrument, a trading halt, and a silently expired multicast join are indistinguishable at instrument level without channel heartbeats.
Instrument-level silence is always benign, because any real feed failure raises a socket error that the poll loop observes on the very next iteration.
Silence is only meaningful once the arbitration window has expired, which makes any additional per-instrument staleness timer entirely redundant.
Instruments carry no timestamps of their own, so there is no per-instrument clock against which an interval of silence could ever be measured.
questions.explanation: Silence is not an error condition: an illiquid option quiet for an hour and an IGMP join that expired ten minutes ago produce byte-identical evidence at the instrument level, which is why detection has to be layered from channel heartbeats, per-instrument activity baselines, cross-feed corroboration, and exchange-versus-local timestamp skew. The socket-error answer is the tempting one and is exactly backwards — the socket stays open and healthy when a multicast join lapses or a publisher stalls, which is what makes the failure silent. Instruments do carry exchange timestamps; the problem is that no message means no timestamp.

questions.prompt: A single-venue book you maintain shows a best bid of 100.04 against a best ask of 100.03. What does this establish?
options: Your book is wrong, because the matching engine would already have executed those orders and this state is structurally impossible at one venue.
The market has locked and the venue will resolve it in the next auction, so the instrument should be marked stale rather than treated as corrupt.
The ask update was applied before the corresponding bid update, so the condition clears on the next message and requires no handler action.
The bid side is holding an order that already executed, which is harmless because filled orders are removed lazily on the following update.
questions.explanation: Within one venue a crossed book cannot exist — the engine would have matched — so the assertion `best_bid >= best_ask` is proof of a defect in your own state and is the cheapest correctness check in the whole system. The 'locked market' answer misstates the definition: locked is bid equal to ask, whereas bid above ask is crossed, and neither is something a continuous single-venue book resolves on its own. There is no lazy-removal semantics that would justify a stale executed order sitting at the top of book.

questions.prompt: Which situation can produce a genuinely crossed book that is not evidence of a bug in your handler?
options: A consolidated view assembled across venues, where one venue's best bid can legitimately exceed a different venue's best ask.
A single venue's continuous book during a burst of aggressive orders, before the matching engine works through its inbound queue.
A single venue's book in the moments after a large Execute message, until the matching Delete for that order finally arrives.
A single venue's book while one of its two sides is still being rebuilt from a depth-truncated snapshot during a resync.
questions.explanation: The legitimate exceptions are consolidated cross-venue books, auction and halt states, and venues that publish implied prices crossing the outright book; these must be enumerated explicitly rather than used as an excuse to weaken the assertion. The 'engine has not caught up' option is the most persuasive distractor because it sounds like a plausible race, but the venue publishes book state as of the engine's own processing, so what it publishes is never crossed. A half-rebuilt book is likewise not an exception — a crossed state during resync is exactly the wrong book the check exists to catch.

questions.prompt: A gap is confirmed on one instrument and snapshot resync is under way. What must the strategy be able to observe, and what must it do?
options: A per-instrument state of SUSPECT or RECOVERING that forbids quoting until the snapshot is installed and the buffer has been drained.
A single global feed-health flag that halts quoting on the entire channel until every instrument carried on it is confirmed LIVE again.
The last known good book with its age attached, so that quotes can be widened in proportion to how stale the state has become.
Nothing at all: the handler should simply stop publishing updates for that instrument until the recovery has finished cleanly.
questions.explanation: The design idea of this section is making 'I do not know the state of this instrument' a first-class representable state that the strategy reads and obeys, which is why recovery is modelled as LIVE / SUSPECT / RECOVERING / DISABLED per instrument. The 'stop publishing' answer is the canonical antipattern: an absent update is indistinguishable from a quiet market, so the strategy carries on quoting a book it believes is current. Widening quotes still means quoting a book known to be wrong, and a global channel halt discards the whole point of per-instrument `RptSeq` recovery.

questions.prompt: Why capture raw packets with hardware timestamps rather than your own normalized event records?
options: A decoded capture already embeds your decoder's bugs, so it can neither validate a decoder change nor reproduce a decoding fault.
Decoded events lack hardware timestamps, because normalization always replaces the wire timestamp with a host clock read at decode time.
Raw packets compress far more effectively than normalized records, which is what makes retaining a full trading day economically feasible.
Normalized events cannot be fed back through the system at all, because the production code path accepts only wire-format input buffers.
questions.explanation: The raw byte stream is the only artifact with lasting value: it is the actual input to the system under test, so a fixed decoder can be re-run against it and a suspected decode bug can be reproduced exactly. The timestamp answer is the closest miss — normalized records commonly do carry the hardware timestamp alongside the host one, so the argument does not turn on timestamps at all but on the fact that decoded records have already passed through the component you are trying to test. Compression economics and injection mechanics are secondary at best.

questions.prompt: You need per-stage latency percentiles for the feed handler measured from a recorded trading day. Which replay mode fits?
options: Paced to the original inter-packet timing, so queueing behaviour and burst structure match what the system actually experienced.
As fast as possible, since removing the idle intervals between packets strips out noise and yields cleaner per-message latency figures.
Accelerated by a fixed factor, which preserves proportional timing between packets and therefore reproduces absolute latencies exactly.
Injected at the wire from a second host, which is the one mode that makes pacing unnecessary because the network supplies the timing.
questions.explanation: Latency is dominated by queueing and burst structure, so the measurement is only meaningful when inter-packet deltas are reproduced; as-fast-as-possible replay is for regression and book validation, where only the final state matters. The accelerated-by-a-factor option is the tempting near-miss: proportional compression is right for load testing, but scaling the intervals changes the queue occupancy at every stage, so absolute latencies are not preserved. Wire injection still needs a pacing decision — the injecting host chooses the rate.

questions.prompt: Which defect can be reproduced only by replaying onto a real network into the real NIC, and not by injecting at the application layer?
options: A receive-ring overflow under a burst, because application injection bypasses the NIC, the driver or bypass library, and the poll loop.
A book-building error in the price-level shift logic, which depends only on the ordering of the decoded messages it is handed.
A non-deterministic merge caused by iterating a hash map when publishing book updates to downstream consumers.
An off-by-one in the snapshot-plus-delta admission condition that discards snapshots which were in fact usable.
questions.explanation: Wire-level injection is the only mode that exercises everything below the application — the NIC, the driver or kernel-bypass library, the ring, and the poll loop — so it is the only way to reproduce ring overflow or a hardware-timestamping fault. The book-shift, hash-iteration, and off-by-one defects are all decisions made above the transport on already-received messages, which is why an application-level harness reproduces them perfectly well and offering one of them here is the natural mistake. Choosing wire injection for those cases buys fidelity you do not need at a large cost in setup.
